The Battle Hymn of the Republic | Jimmy Cajoleas

I used to know a girl who could detach her own head.

I used to know a girl who could detach her own head. She was the sister of my least favorite friend, eight years old to our ten. Louise would get upset over something, like being forced to finish her carrots before she was allowed any of her mother’s famous banana pudding, and her head would detach and go flying around the room. Not only her head, either, but Louise’s throat too, esophagus dangling like a kite string. Her head would circle the room in an angry flutter until her parents acquiesced, plopped a blob of banana pudding on a plate, and chided her for ruining yet another outfit with the thin ribbon of blood that always dribbled down her neck.

Believe me, I witnessed it many times over the years. Why else would I have spent so many afternoons hanging around her brother, with his buckteeth and endless prattle? I loved, for instance, playing Mario Kart late into the night, when I would hear a sound like a large mosquito next to my ear, and look up to see Louise buzzing above me, watching us play. (I mean, rather, Louise’s head, her body still snuggled asleep in her bed.) Louise would stick her tongue out at me and we’d laugh, her brother shouting at her to get lost. She’d sail off down the hallway, stray blood drops dotting the carpet.

Glory, glory, hallelujah. Her truth is marching on.

Her parents tried to keep Louise’s gift a secret. You can do your little trick in front of friends and family, they told her, but never outside the house. Louise abided by their law, for the most part, until a trip to the Saint Patrick’s Day parade one March when she was twelve. The parade was our town’s only annual tradition, and it was packed with drunken adults hollering for beads, children on shoulders, little plastic shamrocks flying everywhere. When the beauty pageant queen passed by on her mermaid float, Louise, who was short for her age, detached her head so she could see. I was there too, eating a turkey leg. I was always there. Watching that pigtailed head bob like a cork in the sky.

Louise made the local news that day. Her parents were mortified. They locked Louise up in her second-story bedroom. Bars over the windows, no schooling, no friends allowed. It was appalling to me, this girl only two years younger than me, imprisoned like Rapunzel in a shitty suburban tower. I rode my bike to their house on summer nights, climbed the tree outside her window, and listened to her sing through the bars, her high brittle voice rising out to the clouds. I tried to keep a low profile during these midnight rendezvous, so I was amazed when she spoke to me one night in July.

“Why are you always in that tree, listening to me? Don’t you think that’s weird?”

I was too nervous to reply.

“Okay, fine. Have any requests?”

I said “Battle Hymn of the Republic.” It was the first thing that popped into my head. Louise sang it for me in her little bird voice. Glory, glory, hallelujah. Her truth is marching on.

By autumn, I knew I had to get her out of her bedroom prison. I stole my older brother’s Jeep Wrangler and drove to Louise’s house. I climbed the oak tree in front of her window and tied the Jeep’s winch cable to the window bars. Back behind the wheel, I threw the Jeep into reverse and yanked the bars from the window. I thought maybe Louise could climb down the tree, the way I’d climbed up, and I could take her back to my house and convince my parents to adopt her. I would be a hell of a lot better of an older brother than her own shitty one, who played as Bowser and always seemed to pull the red shell.

But that wasn’t Louise’s way. She did not climb down the tree, and she did not run away with me and become my sister. Instead, I saw her head, entrails dangling, dart through the window into the chilling September night. I watched her head fly high and higher, up to the stars in their glimmer, until she crossed the moon and vanished from my sight. Down below, I waved my arms
